records.current_fact_excerpt: [F3] For real tests, the field formula and $[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I$ imply $[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=2i\operatorname{Im} \langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2I$. [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]

current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.2.1: 2.1 Let $f,g$ be real tests supported in the two spacelike-separated regions. By [F2] their field commutator is zero. Fact [F3], obtained by expanding the fields with the CCR, then gives $2i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2I=0$; hence the imaginary part vanishes. Substituting it in [F1] gives $W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)=W_\mu(f+g)=W_\mu(g)W_\mu(f)$. Taking adjoints shows each generator from the first region commutes with each generator and adjoint from the second. Commutation is preserved under finite linear combinations and products; if bounded sequences $A_n\to A$ and $B_n\to B$ in operator norm satisfy $A_nB_n=B_nA_n$, then continuity of multiplication gives $AB=BA$. Taking the two norm closures proves the assertion for the full local algebras. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

records.current_fact_excerpt: [F5] The antisymmetric Fock sectors, finite-particle domain, creation formulas, and CAR relations use the conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. By [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]], $\mathcal H_\pm$ are separable, so their finite direct sum $\mathcal K=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$ is separable (take pairs from countable dense sets); with Countable Choice [A1], the hypotheses of the CAR supplier hold for $H=\mathcal K$.

current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.3.1: 3.1 By steps 2.1 and 2.2 the particle and conjugate antiparticle test maps extend to unitaries on $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Their direct sum $T(\tilde g)$ is unitary. Define $U(\tilde g)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T(\tilde g)^{\otimes_a n}$ on the antisymmetric Fock sectors. Each tensor power is unitary by its isometric action on elementary tensors and inverse tensor power; it commutes with the signed permutation average and therefore restricts to a unitary on the antisymmetric sector. The direct sum is unitary and fixes $\Omega$. On elementary wedge tensors the insertion/contraction formulas of [F5] give $U c^\dagger(h)U^{-1}=c^\dagger(Th)$ and $U c(h)U^{-1}=c(Th)$; density extends these identities to the finite-particle domain. Thus $U(\tilde g)\Psi(F)U(\tilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\tilde g}F)$. Direct substitution in the affine and spinor formulas gives $\tau_{\tilde g_2}\tau_{\tilde g_1}=\tau_{\tilde g_2\tilde g_1}$: the coordinate argument is $(\Lambda_2\Lambda_1)^{-1}(x-a_2-\Lambda_2a_1)$ and the matrix factor is $(S_2S_1)^{-\dagger}=S_2^{-\dagger}S_1^{-\dagger}$. By [F8] the Lorentz factors compose within $SO^+(1,3)$; by the definition of $\widetilde G$ its triples are closed under this product. Hence $T$ and its Fock lift $U$ obey the same product law and $U$ is a representation. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F8, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]
current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.4.1: 4.1 The map $\tilde g\mapsto\tau_{\tilde g}F$ is continuous in Schwartz seminorms for each $F$, since it is composition with affine maps and finite matrices whose entries vary continuously. By the continuous test estimate of [F4], the one-particle representation is continuous on the dense test-generated subspaces of step 2.2; its operators have norm one, so approximation extends strong continuity to all one-particle vectors. On an elementary $n$-tensor, the difference of $T(g)^{\otimes n}$ and $T(g_0)^{\otimes n}$ is a sum of $n$ terms, each bounded by the norm of one factor difference times the norms of unchanged factors. It tends to zero as $g\to g_0$. Density and the unit norm bound extend this to each completed antisymmetric sector; finite-sector truncation then extends strong continuity to their direct sum. [F4, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]
current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.4.2: 4.2 By step 2.2 the ranges of $F\mapsto P_+u_F$ and $F\mapsto\overline{P_-u_F}$ are dense in $\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$, respectively. Moreover, $\Psi(F)^\dagger\Omega=c^\dagger(P_+u_F)\Omega$ and $\Psi(F)\Omega=c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F})\Omega$, so their created one-particle components range densely over both summands. For any ordered list of $n$ such fields or adjoints, the all-creation term in their product on $\Omega$ is the wedge of their $n$ creation components. Expand the product into creation and annihilation terms and use the CAR to move every annihilator to the right: a term with a remaining annihilator kills $\Omega$, while each contraction leaves a product with at most $n-2$ creation factors. By induction, those lower-degree wedge vectors are in the polynomial orbit span, so subtracting them isolates the desired degree-$n$ wedge. The degree-zero base also lies in the orbit span: step 2.2 gives a test $F$ with $u_F\ne0$, and the CAR formula of [F4] gives $\{\Psi(F),\Psi(F)^\dagger\}=\|u_F\|^2I$, hence $I$ belongs to the generated algebra. Wedges of vectors from the dense one-particle ranges are dense in each antisymmetric sector by the Hilbert tensor completion, and finite-sector truncations are dense in Fock space. Hence $\Omega$ is cyclic for the global graded field algebra. [F1, F4, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

records.current_fact_excerpt: [F2] On finite-particle vectors, $[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I$ and the sector maps have bounds $\|a_n(h)\|\le\sqrt n\|h\|$, $\|a_n^\dagger(h)\|\le\sqrt{n+1}\|h\|$. [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]

current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.2.1: 2.1 To apply [F2] with one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$, first verify its separability hypothesis. Let $D$ be the countable dense subset of real $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ supplied by [F4]. Its sixfold product is countable by [F5]; identifying each tuple with a three-component complex function whose real and imaginary components lie in $D$ gives a dense subset of $\mathcal H$. Density follows by approximating the six real $L^2$ components, since the squared complex-vector norm is the sum of their squared norms. Hence $\mathcal H$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6]. The image of this countable set under the bounded projection $M_{P_T}$ is countable and dense in $\mathcal H_T$: for $u\in\mathcal H_T$, $M_{P_T}u=u$, so projected approximants to $u$ converge to $u$. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6], and [F2] applies. By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given]
current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.3.1:
3.1 Write $\omega=|\mathbf k|$, and use the Fourier convention $\widehat f(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(\mathbf x)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\,d^3\mathbf x$. The expansion implied by the definition of $g_j$ is
$$A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}}\left(a_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}+a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right),$$
$$E_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=-\partial_0A_i(x^0,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}\left(\frac{\omega}{2}\right)^{1/2}\left(ia_i(\mathbf k)e^{-i\omega x^0+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}-ia_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)e^{i\omega x^0-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}\right).$$
Smearing the first line with $j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb R^3)$ gives exactly $a(g_j)+a^\dagger(g_j)$: the annihilation term uses conjugate-linearity of $a$, while the creation term is linear in its argument.
Here the formula is for $\mathbf k\ne0$; values at $\mathbf k=0$ are irrelevant to the integrals. The symbols $a_i(\mathbf k)$ and $a_i^\dagger(\mathbf k)$ are distributional notation for the Fock maps: for Schwartz vectors $u,v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^3$ set $a(u):=a(P_Tu)$ and $a^\dagger(v):=a^\dagger(P_Tv)$. Then [F2] gives $[a(u),a^\dagger(v)]=\int\overline{u_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)v_j(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k\,I$, equivalently the kernel notation $[a_i(\mathbf k),a_j^\dagger(\mathbf q)]=P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\delta^3(\mathbf k-\mathbf q)I$. The mode integrals are understood after test smearing; near $\mathbf k=0$ their squared one-particle weights behave respectively as $1/\omega$ and $\omega$, both locally integrable against $d^3\mathbf k$, and at infinity the Fourier transforms of the spatial tests decrease rapidly. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given, algebra]
current_actual_proof_use_excerpts.4.1:
4.1 For real $f,h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, define the equal-time spatial smearings by pairing the mode distributions with the spatial tests, $A(f):=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^3}f_i(\mathbf x)A_i(0,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x$ and $E(h):=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^3}h_j(\mathbf y)E_j(0,\mathbf y)\,d^3\mathbf y$. The one-particle vectors in these definitions are
$$g_f(\mathbf k)=\frac{P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat f(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}(2\omega)^{1/2}},\qquad e_h(\mathbf k)=-i\frac{\omega^{1/2}P_T(\mathbf k)\widehat h(\mathbf k)}{(2\pi)^{3/2}2^{1/2}}.$$
These belong to $\mathcal H_T$ by the preceding bounds, and $A(f)=a(g_f)+a^\dagger(g_f)$, $E(h)=a(e_h)+a^\dagger(e_h)$. The CCR [F2] gives
$$[A(f),E(h)]=-i\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3}\,\overline{\widehat f_i(\mathbf k)}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat h_j(\mathbf k)\,I.$$
For real $f,h$, this Fourier integral is real because $P_T$ is real and even and $\widehat f(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat f(\mathbf k)}$, $\widehat h(-\mathbf k)=\overline{\widehat h(\mathbf k)}$.
Equivalently, as a tempered distribution in $\mathbf z=\mathbf x-\mathbf y$,
$$[A_i(0,\mathbf x),E_j(0,\mathbf y)]=-iK_{ij}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),\qquad K_{ij}(\mathbf z)=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf z}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
The last integral defines a tempered distribution because $P_T$ is measurable and bounded: for $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^3)$ its pairing is $(2\pi)^{-3}\int P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)\widehat\varphi(-\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k$, which is absolutely convergent. Since the Fourier symbol of $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla)$ is $P_{T,ij}(\mathbf k)$, this distribution is exactly $P_{T,ij}(-i\nabla_{\mathbf x})\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)$. The sign is negative because $E=-\partial_0A$: the annihilation/creation cross terms contribute $-i/2$ each at equal time. Thus the stated equal-time commutator holds distributionally after smearing, with its stated sign. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, given] ∎

$$[F(h),F(k)]=[a(g_h)+a^\dagger(g_h),a(g_k)+a^\dagger(g_k)] =(\langle g_h,g_k\rangle_2-\langle g_k,g_h\rangle_2)I =2i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle g_h,g_k\rangle_2\,I.$$
